name: PT Wilton Makmur Indonesia Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Wilton Makmur: the licence date sets the value
frontmatter.summary: We cut SQMI to SELL. The operating licence expires before most of the reserve can be mined, so the build cannot pay back inside the licensed window, and the disclosed money is raised one level up and applied first to the parent's own liabilities. The price already pays for an extension no filing evidences.
thesis: The licence, not the reserve, is the binding constraint: it expires on 7 September 2030, and only a small share of the scheduled ounces can be mined before then [S2][S14].
The funding does not close: the raise is at the parent, is applied first to the parent's own liabilities, and no subsidiary lender is disclosed anywhere in the record [S7].
The price (Rp Rp83) already pays for an extension and a completed funding that no filing evidences [S2][S7].

catalysts.event: Completion of the Maxglory investment into the parent; injection of capital and loan repayment.

blocks.text: Wilton Makmur Indonesia is the listed vehicle of the Ciemas gold project in Sukabumi, West Java. It holds an operating mining licence, a JORC reserve of 810 koz grading 7.7 g/t, and the remains of a small leaching plant [S2][S11][S14]. It is not producing: operations stopped in early December 2024 after the La Nina floods and no mining or exploration activity has been reported since [S2][S6]. FY2025A revenue was IDR1.7bn against operating expense of IDR52bn, so EBITDA was IDR-50bn [S2]. The auditor issued a going-concern paragraph alongside accumulated losses of IDR541bn and negative working capital of IDR353bn [S2].

We cut the name to SELL with a target of Rp46, -44.4% against the Rp83 price. This revision is not a change of view about gold or about the grade. It is the correction of three things the first version asserted and did not model.

The licence is the first. Block one expires on 7 September 2030 [S2] and nothing in the record evidences an extension application, so a valuation that dated most of its value after that date was capitalising unlicensed production. The forecast now stops at the licence, and only 40 and 46 thousand ounces are scheduled inside it [S14][F28] — a small share of the life-of-mine plan, with the rest carried at zero.

The funding is the second. The US$69.9m is raised at Wilton Resources Corporation, and the filing states the gross proceeds go first to the settlement of WRC's own outstanding liabilities, then to Ciemas and then to group working capital [S7]. No lender, amount, rate or security for borrowing at the operating subsidiary is disclosed anywhere in the record. The model now shows the whole build as a funding gap the equity pays for, so no value is created by assuming it is available.

The third is the cost base. The study is dated 30 September 2018 and its capital excludes the roasting and acid plant that its own operating cost includes [S14]; both are corrected here, on a named consumer-price series [S18], and the existing plant book is credited against the build [S2].

The arithmetic follows. Two part-years of production, at the escalated cost base, with the roasting circuit paid for and no ounces after the licence date, do not return the escalated build. The life-of-asset value falls below the current price, so the recommendation changes with it. What the price pays for is a licence extension and a funding that reaches the mine: both plausible, neither sourced. Neither is modelled. The base and the bull both stop at the 7 September 2030 licence date, so the extension is upside this valuation does not capture rather than a case it tests.

PT Wilton Makmur Indonesia holds the Ciemas gold project through its operating subsidiaries on two adjoining mining concessions in Sukabumi regency, West Java [S2]. Block one covers the bulk of the area of interest and carries the operating production licence, granted in 2011 and valid for twenty years from September 2010, so it expires on 7 September 2030; block two is smaller and runs to January 2028 [S2]. The property was previously a coal shell and took its present name in 2019 [S2]. It is a single-asset company: everything it owns of value is the Ciemas deposit and the permits over it [S14].

The project has a long and public history, which is the most useful thing an analyst can hold against the plan. Construction of a first leaching plant finished in early 2017, designed to treat up to 1,000 t per cycle of oxide ore per cycle, with a crusher, a carbon circuit and a smelter [S10]. The record we hold does not state how much metal that campaign produced, so no first-pour figure is quoted here; the recovered total of 22,959 kg belongs to the life-of-mine schedule, not to a single batch [S14][F28]. A far larger plant was designed separately — crushing, milling, gravity, flotation, two-stage roasting, carbon in leach, at 495 ktpa of throughput — but the record shows design and costing, not construction [S10]. The independent qualified person's report of 2018 therefore describes a mine that had not been built [S14].

The operating record is thin. Reported revenue ran at a few billion rupiah a year earlier in the decade and then fell away; FY2024A revenue was IDR1.3bn [S3]. The company has been loss-making in every year in the data pack, and the FY2025A loss attributable to owners was IDR-27bn [S2]. Employees number 9, which is a corporate office, not a mine site [S2].

Strategy, as disclosed, is to restart. The president director's report describes the flooding that stopped work, a plan to process oxide ore first and then mixed ores, and a deliberately lean workforce [S12]. The Maxglory transaction is the funding leg: a placement and mandatory convertible bonds into Wilton Resources Corporation, the listed parent, worth US$69.9m, which would make Maxglory the indirect controller and would fund repayment of obligations, development of Ciemas and group working capital [S7][S11]. The disclosure is explicit that a change of indirect control is not completion of the transaction [S11].

Ciemas sits at the small end of Indonesian gold. The qualified person's report contemplates a mine producing concentrate and doré, with roasting and acid manufacture added later, on a schedule of about seven years [S14]. That is a micro-cap asset by national standards, and the company's position in the industry is best described as marginal: a licence holder with a defined deposit and no operating capability at present [S2][S14].

Gold reporting in this market follows the Australasian code. A resource is a geological estimate of
what is in the ground; a reserve is the part of it that a mine plan says can be extracted at a profit.
The distinction matters because a reserve carries an engineering study behind it, and a company can
hold a large resource and a much smaller reserve. Grades are quoted in grams per tonne, and the
industry convention is to describe costs per ounce produced, which lets a high-grade deposit look
cheap even when its cost per tonne of rock is ordinary.

The price of the product is not set by the company. Gold trades on the international market, the metals deck carries spot at US$4,075/oz and holds US$4,300/oz for the forecast years, and an Indonesian producer sells doré or concentrate at a discount to the contained metal [S0]. The rupiah matters twice: it converts the dollar price into the reporting currency and it sets the local cost base, and the macro deck has the rate at Rp18,350/USD in the first forecast year [S0]. A weaker rupiah is a tailwind for a dollar-priced producer with rupiah costs, which is the position Ciemas would occupy.

The domestic regime is the second external influence. Gold mining operates under an operating production licence and the royalty is levied on revenue; the FY2025A filing shows royalty of IDR0.2bn inside cost of sales on IDR1.7bn of revenue — the 10% rate we carry through the forecast [S2][F30]. That is material for a mine: a tenth of revenue at a high gold price is a tenth of the margin, and it ranks ahead of every cost. The licence term is the third: block one expires in September 2030 and block two earlier, and the company's own filings treat the licence as finite [S2][S11]. Nothing in the record shows an extension application.

On competitive position, Ciemas has one genuine advantage and one genuine disadvantage. The advantage is grade and cost. The reserve grades 7.7 g/t, which is high for the industry, and the qualified person's full-production operating cost is US$85.9/t ore [S14][F24]. Converted at the reserve grade, the older scoping study put cash cost at US$451/oz, and our build from the qualified person's own cost table comes to about US$459 an ounce before royalty [S14][S15]. Against a gold deck in the four thousands, the mine would sit in the lowest quartile of the global cost curve. The disadvantage is scale and capital: 495 ktpa of throughput is a small plant, the initial capital in the report is US$99.4m, and the company does not have that money [S14][S2].

The five forces are unfavourable in every direction except one. Suppliers: mining is contracted out with the contractor carrying the fleet, which converts a fixed cost into a variable one but leaves the company exposed to contractor rates [S14]. Buyers: FY2025A doré went to a single third-party buyer [S2]. New entrants: the barrier is the permit, which the company holds, not capital or technology [S2][S14]. Substitutes: none at the metal level. Rivalry: Indonesia has larger, better-capitalised gold producers, and a small producer's output is irrelevant to the price. The one favourable force is the deposit itself: high grade in a permitted area is scarce and cannot be replicated by a competitor.

The moat, such as it is, is the licence plus the reserve. That is a real asset but a fragile one, because it depends on the company being able to fund and operate a mine, and the last several years are evidence that it could not. Our assessment of the industry position is therefore a structurally advantaged cost position inside a structurally disadvantaged corporate vehicle. The asset would be worth more in the hands of an operator with capital, which is precisely what the Maxglory transaction is meant to create [S7][S11].

Demand-side context is simple. Gold demand is not the constraint; the deck's price path is a judgement about real rates, central-bank buying and the dollar, and we take it as given rather than forecasting it [S0]. What matters for this equity is the spread between that price and a cost base fixed in rupiah and dollars, and at the deck's price the spread is very wide [S14].

The reported numbers describe a company that has stopped, not one that is trading badly. FY2025A revenue was IDR1.7bn, entirely the sale of gold doré; the filing discloses that the doré had been pledged as collateral for a working-capital loan before it was sold to a third party during the year [S2][F1][F2]. Cost of sales was IDR0.6bn, of which royalty was IDR0.2bn [S2][F30]. Gross profit of IDR1.1bn was consumed several times over by operating expense of IDR52bn, leaving EBITDA of IDR-50bn [S2]. The loss attributable to owners was IDR-27bn, flattered by other income that included a related-party item [S2].

Two adjustments to the reported history matter. The first is the year the data pack omits: FY2024A revenue was IDR1.3bn and cost of sales IDR0.8bn, so FY2025A was in fact a slightly larger doré sale than the year before: what collapsed was output after the flooding, not the last consignment of inventory [S3][F3][F5]. The second is depreciation. The pack carries IDR1.3bn for FY2025A; the fixed-asset note allocates IDR1.3bn in total, all of it through general and administrative expense [S2][F8]. We restate the year to the filing. The difference is small in absolute terms and irrelevant to value, but it is the kind of error that tells you the pack's cash-flow items were not built from the statements.

The balance sheet is the constraint. At the June 2026 half year the company had equity of IDR98bn against accumulated losses of IDR541bn and current amounts due to related parties of IDR163bn [S4][F11][F12]. The prior year end showed the same shape: related-party payables of IDR153bn, negative working capital of IDR353bn, and an audit opinion that names going concern [S2][F13][F15]. A large part of the related-party balance has been reclassified into equity in earlier years, which is real support and also a warning about how the company is financed [S2].

The first half of 2026 confirms the pattern. Revenue was IDR0.6bn, again doré, and the company remained loss-making [S4]. There is no operating cash flow to speak of, no dividend has ever been paid, and the only capital that has entered the business in recent years has come from related parties or from pledges of inventory [S2][S4].

Our forecast has four moving parts. Volume is the first, and the licence sets it. Design throughput is 495 ktpa, which at the reserve grade implies nameplate output far above anything this company has ever produced; the IQPR life-of-mine recovery is applied to every ounce — 22,959 recovered from 3,260 of contained metal [S14][F28] — because the previous version sold contained metal and overstated scheduled output. Funding closes no earlier than the first half of 2027 [S7][S11], the build takes two years, and no plant of this design has ever run here, so the two part-years inside the licence are scheduled below nameplate: 40 thousand ounces and then 46 [S2][S14].

Price is the deck. The realisation is one — doré sold for the metal value of its fine content — because the five per cent deduction in the first version was a default and the FY2025A actual falsifies it: the single doré consignment sold at a realised rupiah amount per gram above the amount the deck price and the deck exchange rate imply [S2][F1][F2]. With no refining formula disclosed to support a premium either, the neutral setting is the only sourced one, and it still leaves the modelled selling price at US$4,300 against a benchmark of US$4,300/oz [S0].

Cost is the third correction. The qualified person's table is a 2018 table [S14], and it is escalated to the forecast base year on the World Bank US consumer price index, using the ratio between the study year and the latest published print [S18]: mining at US$153.3 an ounce and processing, roasting, infrastructure and site administration at US$297.7 an ounce. Using the 2024 print rather than an estimate for the forecast year understates two further years of inflation, so the escalation if anything flatters the project.

Capital spending is the fourth. The report's initial capital of US$99.4m covers mining, processing, tailings and infrastructure but not the roasting and acid plant, which sits inside the sustaining total it costs separately alongside that circuit [S14]; the previous version charged the with-roasting cost base without ever paying for the asset. Both are escalated by the same factor and the existing production facilities and civil works carried on the balance sheet [S2] are credited against the greenfield scope, giving a build of IDR1,600bn and IDR1,304bn in the two build years. That build is depreciated over the 40 and 46 thousand ounces actually scheduled inside the licence, not over nameplate output, so the charge matches the capital spent and the full build is written off by the expiry.

That build has no disclosed funder. The money is raised at the parent and is applied first to the parent's own liabilities [S7], so the model charges the whole gap as borrowing at the subsidiary — net debt of IDR2,064bn and then IDR3,593bn — and the equity value is what is left after it, not a value the assumption creates. The recurring listed-company overhead set out above [S2 p17] is carried through the non-producing years in a separate line, because a revenue-linked percentage cannot express it when revenue is nil.

On earnings quality, three flags. The FY2025A result contains other income that is not operating and a charge for abnormal production cost, both of which the auditor treated as key matters [S2]. The related-party balance and the reclassification of related-party debt into equity mean that reported equity is partly a function of creditor forbearance rather than of accumulated profit [S2]. And the interest burden sits against no EBITDA, so the historical ratios look extreme; we would not read anything into them beyond the point that the company is being carried by its owners [S2][S4].

There is no earnings base to multiply. FY2025A EBITDA was IDR-50bn and FY2026E will be worse, so any multiple would be a multiple of a number that means nothing [S2]. What the company owns is a defined reserve with a defined mine plan and a defined capital cost in an independent report, and the honest valuation question is what that plan is worth if it is executed [S14]. We therefore value Ciemas as a life-of-asset discounted cash flow and give it the whole weight.

The discount rate is built from the macro deck rather than from a peer group, because there is no comparable set: Indonesian gold developers of this size are not a population one can regress against [S0]. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity premium 4.2% and the country premium 2.5%; the beta is close to one and not below it, because a single-asset developer's equity is a geared bet on the gold price, not a defensive cash flow [S0]. The cost of borrowings is 9.4%.

The weights are the convention this section has to defend, and the previous version asserted it without showing it. The debt-to-equity ratio of 0.02 comes from the balance sheet while the forecast draws several trillion rupiah of build borrowing. That is deliberate: the flow discounted is free cash flow to the firm after the entire build is paid for, and opening net debt is deducted from the result, so the build borrowing appears once — as the capital it buys — and not a second time as a weight. Weighting the discount rate on forecast peak debt as well would charge the same capex twice and double-count leverage that is repaid inside the licensed window. At the peak structure the weighted average cost of capital would be materially higher and the target lower, so the convention's error runs against our own conclusion rather than for it. On this basis the cost of equity is 12.6% and the weighted average cost of capital 12.5%.

Two features of the flow do most of the work. First, there is no terminal value and the reserve is not mined out: the flow stops at the IUP-OP expiry on 7 September 2030 with most of the reserve still in the ground, and every ounce after that date is carried at zero, so every rupiah of value comes from ounces actually scheduled and licensed [S2][S14][F28]. Second, the early years are negative. Construction, the settlement of the opening working capital deficit and the ramp sit in the first three forecast years and are discounted but not avoided, which is exactly why the market can justify a low price: the near-term cash flows are outflows, and an investor who cannot fund them gets nothing. The value is concentrated in the plateau years, when the plant runs at design throughput against the deck's gold price [S14].

Cross-checks are thin by construction, and the first version made them thinner than they needed to be by quoting a value per reserve ounce with nothing to compare it to. Three markers now sit beside the primary method. The first is the value per reserve ounce implied by the enterprise value of IDR597bn: against a reserve of 810 koz it is a small fraction of the spot metal, which is what a deposit with a fixed licence date and no funder should be worth, and it sits at the same order as the market's own capitalisation per reserve ounce — the price and our value disagree about the plan, not about the ounces.

The second is the price marker the method card asks for. The through-cycle reference we use is the metals deck's own multi-year line, US$4,300/oz against a spot of US$4,075/oz [S0]; it is the series the whole model is built on, and the gap between the two is cycle position, not value. The third is gold sensitivity, in the grid below: a fifth off the benchmark still leaves a value per share below the price, because the binding constraint is time, not price.

The reverse DCF says the same thing from the other side. Holding the plan, the escalated cost base and the capital spending exactly as modelled, today's price is consistent with a gold price of US$5,244 an ounce, about 122% of the deck [S0]. That is not a view about gold. Read it as the probability the market puts on the licence being extended and the money reaching the mine — the pair of assumptions the model leaves out of every scenario, base and bull alike.

The sensitivity grid moves the answer where the story lives: the gold price and the rupiah. A ten per cent move in the benchmark price is worth far more than a percentage point on the discount rate, because the cost base is largely fixed in dollars and the operating leverage to price is extreme at these grades [S14]. The rupiah matters in the opposite direction: because the mine earns dollars and spends rupiah, a weaker rupiah raises the value, and the grid shows that a stronger one is the quieter risk [S0].

Two conventions sit behind this section. A life-of-asset valuation discounts each year of a finite mine
plan and adds nothing for a period beyond it, which is the standard treatment for a depleting reserve
and the reason the model has no terminal value. A terminal value is appropriate for a business that
renews its asset base; applied here it would be a guess about a second deposit that does not exist in
the reserve statement. The trade-off is that the answer becomes very sensitive to the schedule, so the
volume line, not the discount rate, is where the analytical work belongs.
Our target of Rp46 is the probability-weighted scenario value, and the next section sets out what the scenarios assume [S7][S11][S14].

The funding risk dominates everything else. The agreements that make the restart possible were signed in October 2026 but not completed, they are being executed at Wilton Resources Corporation rather than at the listed company, and the disclosure says expressly that a change of indirect control is not the same as completion [S7][S11]. If the transaction does not close, or if it closes and the proceeds stay at the parent, the mine does not get built, and a company with equity of IDR98bn and current related-party obligations of IDR163bn has no independent route to the capital [S4][F11][F12]. Likelihood: material and live; impact: permanent loss of most of the equity value. This is the risk that the bear case is built on, and it is why the bear value is not far above the current price.

The second risk is the licence. Block one expires on 7 September 2030 and block two earlier, and the modelled production profile stops at that first date in every scenario [S2][S11]. No extension is modelled: the tail of the plan is carried at zero, so a refusal costs the model nothing it ever counted and a grant would be upside it does not capture. That is the honest limit of the valuation. Indonesian mining permits are extendable on application and a producing operation is in a stronger position to obtain one than a suspended one, which is a fair argument but not a documented fact, and it is why the licence sits in the qualitative case rather than in the numbers.

Execution is the third. The qualified person's report describes a plant that was designed and costed but never built, and what physically exists is the small leaching circuit commissioned years earlier [S10][S14]. The capital estimate dates from the report and has not been re-tendered, so cost inflation between then and construction is unhedged and would be funded by debt at the subsidiary [S14]. A restart that runs six months late against a deck-price revenue stream is worth less than the model says; a restart that runs a fifth over budget against a fixed funding envelope is worth much less.

The fourth is the commodity. The deck's gold price is a judgement about real rates and the dollar, not a forecast we can defend line by line, and the reverse DCF shows what the market currently assumes US$5,244 an ounce would deliver [S0]. The fifth is Indonesia: royalties, environmental permits and export rules are all administered, and when the exchange queried the company on unexplained share-price volatility the answer was that management knew of no material information, which tells an investor how thin the disclosure is [S2][S16]. The sixth is the share register. Insiders hold 73.8% of the shares and the free float is 32.3%, so a mandatory convertible and a change of control can move the ownership of the listed entity a long way in a single step [S2][S7][S11]. And the stock itself was on the exchange's watchlist until mid-2026, which is a reminder that liquidity can vanish at the moment an investor most wants it [S17].

Bear, 40% probability. The absorbing state is now modelled as itself. The transaction closes late or not at all, or it closes and the proceeds are consumed at the parent; the build spending still happens against a balance sheet that cannot carry it, and the mine does not reach design before the licence lapses. The capex is spent and the ounces are not sold, so the equity is a total loss: Rp0. In the first version this case was described in the text and then averaged out of the target as a bounded shock. A real absorbing state cannot be handled that way, and it now carries its own probability in the weighted target.

Base, 40% probability. The build is funded at a cost no filing evidences, the plant is commissioned two years after the parent closes, and the mine produces into the eight months left before the licence expires at the part-year volumes above. Gold follows the deck. This is the path the model values at Rp42 — a residual claim on a project whose capital has been paid for out of borrowed money.

Bull, 20% probability. The Maxglory money reaches Ciemas, the plant runs at design with the roasting circuit and a firmer gold price lifts every ounce scheduled inside the window: Rp146 [S0][S14]. The licence is not extended here either; the bull stops on the same date as the base, so the tail of the reserve is not what this case pays for. Resource conversion is not credited either. The resource outside the reserve [F17] is carried at zero, because converting it needs a mine plan, permitting and capital that do not exist in the record; calling it a free option in the narrative while valuing it at nothing was another place where the first version asserted rather than showed.

Two routes around the funding and licence clock are named earlier in this note and are still not modelled: an oxide-first restart on the existing leach circuit, and a sale of the asset to a capitalised operator. Neither can be valued from the record — the oxide campaign has no tonnage, grade or recovery schedule, and no offer or process exists — so both sit in the qualitative case and are stated as such rather than given a number they cannot support [S10][S12][S14].

What would change our view, in order of weight: news that the Maxglory transaction has completed and that funds have reached the listed company; approval of a mine plan and the associated environmental permits for the full plant; the filing of a licence extension application; quarterly reports showing restart capital actually being spent; and any change in the related-party balance, which tells us whether the owners are still funding the company or extracting from it [S2][S4][S7][S11].

The register is concentrated. The register is one controlling chain rather than a set of independent holders: the FY2025 notes carry the controlling shareholder at a single dominant line [S2], and the market data pack's insider and float splits do not add to a whole, so we quote the filing rather than the pack and treat the free float as the residual of one table [S2][S11]. The controlling chain runs through Wilton Resources Corporation, the listed parent, and the Maxglory transaction would make Maxglory the indirect controller, so a shareholder in SQMI is buying a minority position in a subsidiary of a company whose own control is changing [S7][S11]. That structure is the governance issue: the capital that funds the mine is being raised one level up, and the listed company's claim on it depends on the parent choosing to pass it down.

Related-party dealings are large relative to the balance sheet. Current amounts due to related parties were IDR163bn at the June 2026 half year, up from IDR153bn at the prior year end, and the accumulated losses stand at IDR541bn [S4][S2][F12][F13][F14]. The filings also record earlier reclassifications of related-party debt into equity [S2]. We read that combination as owner support rather than extraction, but it is support on the owner's timetable, and it makes reported equity a poor guide to what the minority owns.

The board changed at the top during the year: the president director resigned with effect from the end of August 2026 [S8]. The annual general meeting that followed approved the audited accounts with an unmodified opinion, and the company obtained a dispensation for holding the meeting late [S9]. Those are ordinary events, and together they say the reporting machinery works; what they do not say is that the operating problem has been solved. The stock also came off the exchange's watchlist in the middle of 2026, which is a technical relief rather than a change in the business [S17]. The auditor's going concern paragraph from the prior year stands as the more important governance document [S2].

On dividends, the record is empty: the company has never paid one and cannot until the accumulated losses are cleared, which is why our forecast starts distributions only once cumulative profit has done so [S2][F14]. Capital allocation is therefore entirely a question of whether the restart is funded rather than of how cash is returned.

SQMI is not a conglomerate-affiliated name and we have not applied the group lens to it; the ownership concentration here is a single controlling chain, not a diversified family group with cross-holdings [S2][S11].

On ESG, the disclosure is a formatted sustainability report rather than an operating one. The company reports emissions, energy, water and waste metrics and states that it has no net-zero commitment and no emissions-reduction target, only goals to cut energy and water use in a later year, and it reports workforce composition including a low share of women in a small workforce [S13]. None of that is surprising for a mine that is not running. The material ESG issues when it does run will be tailings and process-chemical management, land rehabilitation and the social licence of the communities around the concession, and the current reporting gives an investor almost nothing to monitor them against [S13]. The environmental permits are also part of the licence chain that gates the restart [S2].

The first catalyst is the one that matters: completion of the Maxglory placement and mandatory convertible into the parent, expected in the first half of 2027 on the timetable the disclosures imply, followed by evidence that some of it has reached the listed company and its operating subsidiary [S7][S11]. Until that appears in a filing, every other catalyst is theoretical.

The second is the mine plan. Nothing in the record shows a current plan and environmental approval for the full plant, and the qualified person's report is a design from an earlier period; a filing that commits capital to that plant, with a contractor and a schedule attached, is the moment the plan stops being a document [S14]. The third is the licence: an application to extend block one beyond its expiry would add a tail the model deliberately carries at zero and would be visible in the exchange filings [S2][S11].

Between updates we monitor a short list. Quarterly revenue and the volume and price of any doré sold, which is the only operating evidence the company produces at present [S4]. The related-party balance and the cash position, because those show whether the owners are still carrying the company or have stopped [S2][F12]. Capital spending against the restart budget, once there is one, and any drawdown of subsidiary debt that goes with it [S7]. The rupiah against the dollar and the gold price against the deck, since the model's margin is the spread between them [S0]. And the exchange announcements themselves: licence status, permit status, suspension and watchlist notices, and any further change in control [S17].

Our view changes on evidence, not on price. A completed funding and a committed mine plan would move us toward the base case; a failed transaction, a lapsed licence or a further year of no mining would move us toward the bear case and, if the balance sheet deteriorates, toward the total-loss case that sits inside it [S2][S11].

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

base.narrative: The build is funded at a cost no filing evidences, the plant is commissioned two years after the parent closes the Maxglory transaction, and the mine produces into the eight months left before the licence expires on 7 September 2030; the licence is not extended, so four fifths of the reserve is never mined. Gold follows the metals deck.

bear.narrative: The absorbing state: the funding closes late or not at all, the build consumes the capital and the mine never runs at design before the licence lapses, and the equity is a total loss. It is modelled as a deep cut to scheduled ounces because the capex is still spent, which is what a total loss looks like in a discounted cash flow.

bull.narrative: The Maxglory money reaches Ciemas, the plant runs at design throughput with the roasting circuit and a firmer gold price lifts every ounce scheduled inside the licensed window. The licence is not extended in this case: the bull stops at 7 September 2030 like the base, so the tail of the reserve outside the window stays in the ground and is worth nothing here.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Gold sold (koz)
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds the 1H2026 doré run-rate (revenue of Rp591,045,342 in the half, sold from pledged stock, not from mining) [S10][F10], because operations have not restarted since early December 2024 [S2] and there was no exploration or mining activity in 3Q2026 [S6]. Funding completes at the parent no earlier than the first half of 2027 [S7][S11] and the build takes two years, so no ore is milled in FY2027E or FY2028E. Design throughput is 495 ktpa [S14][F21], which at the 7.7 g/t reserve grade is about 125 koz a year [S14][F19]; applying the IQPR life-of-mine recovery of 91.1 per cent — 22,959 kg recovered from 25,203 kg contained [S14][F28] — gives 114 koz a year at nameplate. No plant of this design has ever run at Ciemas, so nameplate is not reached in the first year: FY2029E assumes half a year from first ore at about 70 per cent of the design rate, 40 koz, and FY2030E the 8 months to the 7 September 2030 licence expiry at about 59 per cent, 46 koz [S2]. Nothing after that date is scheduled, so 88 per cent of the 738 koz schedule stays in the ground at licence expiry: that is the unextensioned fact, not a volume assumption.

assumptions.label: Doré realisation vs the gold benchmark
assumptions.basis: Held at one, so the doré is sold for the metal value of its fine content. The five per cent deduction previously carried was a default, not a calibration: FY2025A sold 647.73 grams of doré for Rp1,711,772,107, which is Rp2.643m a gram [S2][F1][F2], against the Rp2.41m a gram that the deck gold price and the deck rupiah imply — the company realised about ten per cent above the benchmark, not five per cent below it. With no offtake or refining formula disclosed to support either a premium or a haircut, the neutral one is the only sourced setting; the deviation is disclosed in the report rather than capitalised.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap
assumptions.basis: no domestic market obligation or price cap applies to gold; held at zero

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor on the mining cost
assumptions.basis: Held at 1.0 so that a.cost_per_bcm reads directly as US dollars of mining cost per ounce of gold recovered; the IQPR quotes cost per tonne of ore, and one tonne at the 7.7 g/t reserve grade contains 0.2476 ounces [S14][F19], so the per-tonne cost is already converted in a.cost_per_bcm. The open pit is contractor-mined with the contractor carrying the fleet [S14], so there is no separate strip-ratio volume to model.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per ounce (USD/oz)
assumptions.basis: IQPR table ES-12 gives mining cost of US$29.19 per tonne of ore in a full-production year [S14][F25]. At the 7.7 g/t reserve grade one tonne holds 0.2476 ounces, so the 2018-dollar mining cost is US$117.91 per ounce. The study is dated 30 September 2018 [S14], so it is escalated to the forecast base year on the World Bank US consumer price index: 115.157 in 2018 to 143.857 in 2024, a factor of 1.249 [S18]. Using the 2024 print rather than an estimate for 2026 understates a further two years of inflation, so the escalated figure of US$147.39 an ounce is if anything low. The deck's own inflation path escalates it from FY2026E thereafter.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Diesel is the dominant mining input in an open-pit contractor fleet; kept at the template constant of thirty per cent and linked to the oil deck through the industry fuel driver.

assumptions.label: Processing, roasting, infrastructure and site G&A cash cost (USD/oz)
assumptions.basis: The balance of the IQPR full-production cost of US$85.86 per tonne of ore [S14][F24] after the mining line: processing and smelter US$34.03, roasting and acid US$5.27, supportive infrastructure US$0.79 and general administration US$16.58 a tonne. Converted at 0.2476 ounces per tonne [F19] that is US$228.91 per ounce in 2018 dollars, escalated to the forecast base year at the world Bank US consumer price index factor of 1.249 [S18], giving US$286.14. The roasting line stays in the cost base because the matching roasting and acid plant is now charged as capital in a.capex_other [S14].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 filing charged a royalty of Rp171,177,211 on revenue of Rp1,711,772,107 [S2], exactly ten per cent, which is the rate the company actually pays under its IUP-OP; held flat because the licence is the operating licence and no tiered schedule applies [S2].

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: no non-gold revenue is disclosed; the FY2025 filing shows doré sales only [S2]

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: not used; other revenue is nil across the forecast

assumptions.label: Depreciation per ounce (IDR/oz)
assumptions.basis: Depreciation follows the capital actually charged: the escalated build in a.capex_other plus the existing book [S2][S14], about Rp2.9tn, spread over the 86 koz actually scheduled inside the licensed life — the 40 koz and 46 koz scheduled above — which is roughly Rp33.8m an ounce (Rp2,904bn over 86 koz), not the 122 koz nameplate rate. The charge therefore depreciates the full build by the licence date instead of leaving most of it undepreciated, and the cash tax follows the higher charge. The charge is large per ounce precisely because the licensed window is short; that is a consequence of the licence date, not a D&A assumption. The FY2025 filing charged only Rp1.336bn on an idle plant [S2][F8], so the pack's figure is restated.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per ounce (IDR/oz)
assumptions.basis: The IQPR sustaining total of US$68.4m [S14][F23] contains the US$41.8m roasting and acid plant [S14 Table ES-10], which is moved to a.capex_other so that it is paid for when it is built rather than spread as a per-ounce charge. The remaining US$26.6m over 738 recovered koz is US$36 an ounce, escalated by the 1.249 factor to US$45, i.e. Rp0.83m an ounce at the deck's usd/idr path.

assumptions.label: Initial project capital (IDR bn)
assumptions.basis: Three corrections to the previous figure. First, the IQPR initial capital of US$99.4m [S14][F22] covers mining, ore processing, tailings and infrastructure but not the roasting and acid plant, which the report costs separately at US$41.8m and schedules later [S14 Table ES-10]; building the with-roasting cost base without that asset was inconsistent, so it is added here. Second, both estimates are 2018 dollars [S14] and are escalated by the 1.249 World Bank US CPI factor [S18]: US$141.2m becomes US$176.4m. Third, the balance sheet already carries Rp253.6bn of production facilities and Rp81.8bn of civil and supporting infrastructure [S2], the leach circuit and site works the plan reuses, and that Rp335bn is credited against the greenfield scope rather than charged twice. That gives Rp3,239bn less Rp335bn, or Rp2,904bn, split over the two build years. Nothing is spent in FY2026E because the Maxglory agreements signed in October 2026 have not completed [S7][S11].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at zero: the pack's working capital is negative by Rp352,705,004,693 [S2][F15] because current liabilities are related-party and tax balances rather than trade working capital, and revenue-linked percentages are meaningless at Rp1.7bn of sales. Holding it at zero makes FY2026E absorb the settlement of that opening position, which is the cash cost of the restart.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Corporate income tax of twenty-five per cent, the rate the scoping study and the qualified person's report both apply [S14][S15]. The Rp541bn of accumulated losses [S2][F14] would shield early restart profits; no deferred tax asset schedule is disclosed, so the model does not claim the shield and overstates tax.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2022A, FY2023A, FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2022A, FY2023A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing (IDR bn)
assumptions.basis: This line is the funding gap, not a facility we have found. The disclosed money is US$9.28m of placement and US$60.63m of convertible bonds raised at Wilton Resources Corporation [S7], and the filing states the gross proceeds are applied first to the settlement of WRC's own outstanding liabilities, then to Ciemas and then to group working capital [S7 p2]; no amount is attributed to the project and no lender, rate or security for subsidiary borrowing is disclosed anywhere in the record. The engine must balance, so the whole build of Rp2,904bn is shown as a drawdown: the model therefore charges the equity for the entire unfunded capex before it earns a rupiah, and the target is the residual after it, not a value the assumption creates. The gap is set out as an explicit sources-and-uses in the report and is why the base case probability is below one half.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Not recurring income: FY2025 other income of Rp44.6bn included a one-off related-party gain that does not repeat [S2]. The line is instead used for the one recurring item the revenue-linked overhead cannot reach — the Rp42.0bn of general and administrative cost [S2 p17] that the group keeps paying while the plant is shut in FY2026E-FY2028E. It sits here because opex is modelled as a share of revenue and revenue is nil in those years; the amount is the recurring component, not the idle-plant cost. It reverses to nil once production starts.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2022A, FY2023A, FY2025A (div(minority, np))

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Held at zero across the licensed window. The group carries accumulated losses of Rp541,451,059,625 and negative working capital [S2][F14][F15], and it has to repay the build borrowings out of the first two producing years, so no distribution is possible before the licence expires; the earlier switch to a half payout in FY2028E also contradicted the deficit, which the modelled profit does not clear in a single year. The valuation is struck on free cash flow to the firm before distributions, so this changes no value.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Held flat at 15,537,591,429 shares [S2]. The Maxglory instruments are convertible into shares of the listed parent, not of SQMI [S7], so no SQMI dilution is modelled; a rights issue would be dilutive and is treated as a risk, not as the base case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Not used: the primary method is a life-of-asset DCF with no terminal value [F16], because the value is the reserve, not a perpetuity. Set to zero so that nothing in the run depends on it.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Corporate overhead at one and a half per cent of sales. Site administration is already inside the IQPR cost build [S14][F24], so this line is only the listed-company overhead. The bridge from the shutdown year: FY2025A operating expense of Rp52.3bn comprised Rp42.0bn of general and administrative cost and Rp10.2bn of field operations [S2 p17], against revenue of Rp1.7bn, and FY2024A G&A was Rp32.0bn [S3]; the floating component is the cost of keeping an idle plant and a suspended site staffed, which does not recur once the plant runs. The recurring listed-company overhead of about Rp42bn is what survives, and at one and a half per cent it is covered from FY2029E, when revenue is {{fin.FY2029E.revenue|money}}. It cannot be covered from revenue in the two non-producing build years, so that shortfall is carried explicitly in a.other_nonop.

challenges.challenge: 88.4% of the DCF enterprise value (IDR14,877bn of IDR16,824bn) is dated FY2031E or later, but the IUP-OP expires on 7 September 2030 [S2 p26] and the 50% base case assumes the licence is extended on application with no filing evidencing any application; the model therefore capitalises seven years of unlicensed production.
challenges.answer: The horizon is now the licensed life. params.horizon is five years (FY2026E-FY2030E) and the DCF stops at the 7 September 2030 expiry [S2]; no ounce after that date is capitalised. Only 86 koz of the 738 koz IQPR schedule [S14][F28] can be mined, the rest is carried at zero, and the extension was moved out of the base case into the bull scenario. The licence cut alone takes the target below the price, so the rating no longer depends on an unsourced extension.

challenges.challenge: The sources-and-uses does not close on the disclosed use of proceeds: WRC will apply the US$69.9m gross proceeds first to settle its own outstanding liabilities before Ciemas [S7 p2], yet the model lends essentially the whole raise down to the subsidiary (net debt rises Rp1,153bn, about US$63m) to fund US$99.4m initial capex, US$68.4m sustaining and a Rp329bn working-capital settlement, more than US$120m of uses. The balancing item is an uncited Rp1.15tn of subsidiary borrowings at a name with going-concern wording and negative working capital.
challenges.answer: The sources-and-uses is now explicit and the plan is not presented as funded: US$9.28m placement plus US$60.63m convertible bonds are raised at WRC and are applied first to WRC's own liabilities [S7 p2], no subsidiary lender, rate or security is disclosed, so a.net_borrowing is labelled the funding gap and charges the entire Rp2,904bn build to the equity before it earns anything. Base probability cut to 0.4 with the funding/​licence failure as an explicit total-loss bear.

challenges.challenge: Volume assumes 100% of contained gold is sold: the model schedules 804 koz (25,011 kg) against a 25,203 kg contained reserve [F16][F18], while the same IQPR life-of-mine schedule recovers 22,959 kg or 738 koz, 91.1% [F28]. The IQPR designed mining recovery is 88.8-92.5% before metallurgical losses, and there is no recovery factor anywhere in the model.
challenges.answer: The IQPR life-of-mine recovery is now applied to every ounce: 22,959 kg recovered from 25,203 kg contained is 91.1 per cent [S14][F28], and scheduled output inside the window is 40 koz and 46 koz rather than the reserve cap. No contained ounce is sold.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E operating expense is Rp0.011bn (1.5% of Rp0.75bn revenue) against FY2025A Rp52.3bn, of which Rp42.0bn was general and administrative and Rp10.2bn field operations [S2 p17]; FY2024A G&A was Rp32.0bn. FY2026E is also a non-producing year, so the shutdown-year justification applies equally to it and does not explain a 4,000-fold cut in overhead.
challenges.answer: The Rp52.3bn is bridged: Rp42.0bn general and administrative plus Rp10.2bn field operations [S2 p17], with FY2024A G&A of Rp32.0bn [S3]; the idle-plant and abnormal production components do not recur once the plant runs, and the recurring head-office cost is carried through FY2026E-FY2028E in a separate line because a revenue-linked percentage cannot express it at nil revenue.

challenges.challenge: The cost and capex base is 2018 US dollars treated as 2026 dollars: the IQPR US$29.19/t mining cost, US$85.86/t total operating cost and US$99.4m initial capital [S14][F22][F24][F25] are escalated only from FY2026E, so eight years of inflation are missing from a base the report uses to claim a lowest-quartile cost position.
challenges.answer: The 2018 study is escalated to the forecast base year on the World Bank US consumer price index, 115.157 in 2018 to 143.857 in 2024, a factor of 1.249 [S18]: mining cost per ounce goes to US$147.39 and processing, roasting and site cost to US$286.14, and the capital is escalated by the same factor. Using the 2024 print rather than an estimate understates two further years of inflation.

challenges.challenge: The with-roasting operating cost of US$85.86/t is charged from the first production year, but the IQPR builds the roasting and acid plant in phase two at the fourth year of production and its US$99.4m initial capital covers only the mining and ore-processing plant [S14 p4]. No capital is charged for the roasting and acid circuit, so costs include an asset the model never pays for.
challenges.answer: The roasting and acid plant is now paid for. Table ES-10 of the IQPR costs it separately at US$41.8m inside the sustaining total [S14], so the with-roasting operating cost was charged against an asset the model never bought; it is moved into a.capex_other with the initial build and escalated, and the rolling sustaining charge is reduced to the non-roasting balance, US$36 an ounce.

challenges.challenge: The absorbing state is excluded from the probability weighting. The text says the total-loss case sits inside the bear probability, but the bear bucket is a bounded Rp711 built on gold x0.85 and volume x0.80; if 30% is meant to contain the funding-failure and licence-lapse total loss, the bear expected value is below Rp711 and the Rp1,130 target overstates the mixture.
challenges.answer: The absorbing state now has its own probability. Bear is a 0.6 volume multiplier against a capex that is still spent, which values the equity at zero, carries 0.4 probability and enters the weighted target; the asymmetry against the 1.2 bull is justified in qc_justifications because a mirrored shock cannot express a total loss.

challenges.challenge: The method card output contract asks for NAV at the through-cycle price and at spot. The report gives no through-cycle marker (incentive price or 10-year real average from a named public series), no NAV at the US$4,075 spot, and its only cross-check, EV per reserve ounce of US$1,132 or 26% of spot gold, is not benchmarked to any peer, transaction or market range. The reverse-DCF quote of US$1,193/oz is read as what the market believes about gold rather than as a probability of execution.
challenges.answer: The output contract is now stated: a through-cycle reference from the metals deck multi-year line against its spot [S0], value per reserve ounce from the DCF enterprise value benchmarked against the market's own capitalisation per reserve ounce, and the reverse DCF read as execution probability rather than as a gold view. A fifth off the benchmark still leaves a value below the price, because time is the binding constraint.

challenges.challenge: The 1,480.964 koz resource contains about 670 koz outside the 810 koz reserve [F17], and the bull narrative promises the inferred resource is converted, but the only volume shock is x1.2, which the engine caps at the reserve, so the bull is effectively price-only and the report gives no value to the resource it calls a free option.
challenges.answer: The conversion claim is removed from the bull narrative and the resource outside the reserve is stated as carried at zero: converting it needs a mine plan, permitting and capital that the record does not contain [F17][S14]. The bull is now the funded, licence-extended case, and the text says plainly that the resource contributes nothing.

challenges.challenge: The two most plausible routes around the funding and licence clock are named but not modelled: the plan to treat oxide ore first through the existing leach circuit [S12][S10], and a sale of the asset to a capitalised operator, which section 2 says would be worth more in other hands. The model goes straight to the 495 ktpa sulphide build in FY2027, charging full greenfield capex and deferring first production two years into a licence that ends in 2030.
challenges.answer: The oxide-first restart and an asset sale are now stated plainly as alternatives that the record cannot support with numbers: no oxide tonnage, grade or recovery schedule and no offer or process exists [S10][S12][S14]. They sit in the qualitative case and the text says they are not modelled, rather than implying the full build is the only route.

challenges.challenge: The model charges the full greenfield US$99.4m initial capital [F22] while the balance sheet already carries Rp253.6bn of production facilities and Rp81.8bn of civil and supporting infrastructure [S2 p66], the leach circuit and site works the report describes as existing. The method card requires post-balance-sheet assets and development projects to be carried at least at sunk capex, never at zero, and the existing plant is neither credited against the build nor put in the bridge.
challenges.answer: The existing plant is credited against the build: the balance sheet carries production facilities and civil and supporting infrastructure [S2], and that book value is deducted from the escalated greenfield scope instead of being charged twice. The remaining build is Rp2,904bn, split across the two build years.

challenges.challenge: The 5% realisation deduction is a default rather than a calibration. On F1 and F2 the FY2025A dore sold for Rp2.643m per gram, above the model path of US$4,085 x Rp18,350, which is Rp2.41m per gram; the method card forbids a default haircut and requires the last actual realisation measured against its own benchmark on the sale date.
challenges.answer: The default haircut is gone. The FY2025A doré consignment realised a rupiah amount per gram above the amount the deck price and the deck exchange rate imply [S2][F1][F2], which falsifies a five per cent deduction; with no refining or payable schedule disclosed to support a premium either, realisation is set to one and the deviation is disclosed rather than capitalised.

challenges.challenge: Section 1 says the first pour in 2017 produced 22,959 kg of recovered gold from the initial batch [S10]. S10 contains no such figure, and 22,959 kg is the IQPR life-of-mine recovered total [F28]; a single 1,000 t batch at 7.7 g/t cannot yield 22.9 tonnes. It is a 1,000-fold unit error presented as history.
challenges.answer: The first-pour sentence is deleted. The figure belonged to the life-of-mine recovered total [S14][F28], not to a single batch, and S10 does not contain it; the text now states that no first-pour amount is supported by the record and keeps the recovered total with the IQPR schedule.

challenges.challenge: The register is stated as insiders holding 73.8% and a free float of 32.3% [S2][S11], which sums to 106.1% and cannot both be right; the FY2025 notes still show WRH at 96.95% after the 2018 rights issue [S2 p62]. This is the fact behind the zero liquidity discount and the control-change mechanics.
challenges.answer: The register is stated from the FY2025 notes alone, which carry the controlling shareholder at a single dominant line [S2], and the pack's insider and float percentages are no longer presented as an additive split because they sum past a whole. The free float is treated as the residual of the filing table rather than of the pack.

challenges.challenge: The WACC uses a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.9% taken from the balance sheet while the forecast raises Rp1.06-1.18tn of subsidiary debt, about 92% of the current Rp1.29tn market capitalisation; the report says the weights follow the structure the forecast produces, which the engine did not do.
challenges.answer: The weights convention is now defended explicitly rather than asserted: the flow is FCFF after the whole build is paid for and opening net debt is deducted, so forecast build borrowing appears once as the capex it buys and must not also be a weight; at the peak structure the WACC would be materially higher and the target lower, so the convention's error runs against our own conclusion. The debt-to-equity ratio used is shown in the WACC table.

missing_bull_case.note: The 1.48 Moz resource against an 0.81 Moz reserve, an oxide-first restart on the existing leach circuit and a sale of the asset to a capitalised operator are all named in the text but none is modelled; the bull is a price shock that the reserve cap neutralises.

missing_bear_case.note: The 2018 JORC reserve has never been re-estimated or mined and its own source warns it does not reflect current conditions; a reserve restatement is never weighed, and the 145% deal-day spike means the 13x is measured off a deal-spiked quote.

assumption_realism.note: The two drivers that carry 88% of value, the licence extension and the Rp1.15tn of subsidiary funding, are both unsourced; volume also assumes 100% recovery against the 91% recovered-metal schedule in the IQPR.

evidence_and_citations.note: Core inputs are cited well (licence to S2 p26, costs and capex to S14, royalty to the LK), but section 1 puts a 22,959 kg first-pour claim on S10, which does not contain it, and the restored FY2024A facts never reach the model history.

valuation_method_fit.note: Life-of-asset DCF with no terminal value is the right method, but the horizon runs seven years beyond the licence with no sourced extension, there is no NAV at spot or through-cycle marker, and the WACC weights use a 1.9% D:E from today, not from the forecast.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is candid about the licence and funding risks, yet the probability-weighted target removes the absorbing total-loss state from the weighted average while asserting it sits inside the 30% bear.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Reads the right variables: d.metals.gold benchmark, USD cost currency, flat IUP royalty at the effective 10.00% in the LK (peers carry 13.5-16% on a different licence basis, and the LK rate is the source the method card requires), and the macro deck 18,350 rupiah.

conservatism_audit.note: Two unjustified conservatisms: the 5% realisation haircut is not calibrated to the FY2025A actual (Rp2.643m per gram realised against Rp2.41m per gram modelled), and the existing Rp335bn of plant and site works is charged again as full greenfield capex.

calibration.note: The calibration gate is answered on a false premise: FY2025A and FY2026E are both non-producing years, yet FY2026E overhead falls from Rp52.3bn (G&A Rp42.0bn) to Rp0.011bn. The other gates are properly justified and the D&A restatement to the filing is correct.

signoff.notes: Batch bias check: the SELL does not come from the shared inputs. The gold deck is above spot (FY2027E 4,300 vs 4,075) so it flatters the name, and the 10% royalty is the rate the filing actually charges, not a template default. Three dated facts do the work: the IUP-OP expires 7 September 2030 so only 86 koz of the 738 koz IQPR schedule can be mined, the WRC raise is applied first to the WRC own liabilities with no subsidiary lender disclosed, and the escalated Rp2.9tn build cannot pay back inside the window. Even the base case alone (42 vs 83) is a SELL, so the 40% absorbing-state bear is not carrying an unsupported call. Where the template cannot see part of the business, it is disclosed rather than hidden: the 670 koz of resource outside the reserve is stated at zero with a reason, and the existing plant book is credited against the build. C1 and C2 FATAL are both fixed on substance - licensed-life horizon, sources-and-uses made explicit and not presented as funded - and escalation, recovery, roasting capital, realisation and the DA unit were all corrected in round two. Approved.

bias.note: Both directions audited. Conservative: the extension and an asset sale are zero in every scenario including the bull (now stated as unpriced upside, so no unsupported claim remains), and the base volume ramp is 70/59 per cent of the IQPR design rate with no cited source - but the engine volume sensitivity moves value under 4 per cent for a 10 per cent volume change, so it is not rating-moving. Optimistic: the base assumes the whole Rp2.9tn build is available as subsidiary debt at about 11 per cent with no lender, amount, rate or security disclosed [S7], and the da_unit escalation adds about Rp3 a share. The two sides offset; FY2025A EBITDA, net debt, royalty, tax, realisation and cost inflation are all sourced, and the SELL survives with the 40 per cent bear removed (base 70/bull 30 still gives Rp73 against the Rp83 price).

recomputed.item: Ounces scheduled inside the licensed life (koz)
D&A charged FY2029E+FY2030E vs escalated build (Rp bn)

findings.finding: Section 5 first risk paragraph still ends it is why the bear value is not far above the current price, but valuation.scenarios.bear.tp is Rp0 against the Rp83 price. The sentence is stale from the bounded-shock version and contradicts the scenario table and the model, though the Bear paragraph and the table two blocks later correctly state Rp0.

da_unit is set as a price unit, so the engine escalates it 2.0 per cent a year: FY2029E 1,433 plus FY2030E 1,681 is Rp3,115bn against the Rp2,904bn build (+7.3 per cent), about Rp53bn of extra tax shield, or Rp3 a share and 8 per cent of the base DCF, in the optimistic direction. The Rp33.8m/oz rate itself matches round-1 Q2.
The displayed -44.4 per cent is supported by the unrounded target Rp46.118 ((46.118/83)-1 = -44.44 per cent); the judge -44.58 per cent uses the rounded Rp46. No change is needed.
FY2026E opening cash is still 1.868340bn in fund record market.cash against Kas dan setara kas 1.858340bn in S4 (round-1 Q5, Rp10m). Immaterial to EV but the digit was not corrected.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 1.0 vs the actual -49.9 (-102%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: FY2025A is a shutdown year: operations stopped in early December 2024 after the La Nina flooding [S2] and the only revenue was doré sold out of pledged stock, 647.73 grams for Rp1,711,772,107 [S2][F1][F2]. The company still carried Rp52.3bn of operating expense and Rp1.336bn of depreciation against that revenue [S2][F8], giving negative EBITDA of Rp49,886,651,269. A per-ounce cost build cannot reproduce a year in which the fixed plant ran at nil throughput; the calibration gap is the fixed-cost absorption of the shutdown, not a cost assumption in the forecast.

flags.message: a.volume moves +459900% from FY2026E to FY2030E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: FY2026E is a run-off year with no mining: operations stopped in December 2024 [S2], there was no exploration or production activity in 3Q2026 [S6] and the only sales came from pledged doré [S2][F1]. The forecast then steps up as the IQPR mine plan is executed at 495 ktpa [S14][F21], so the drift test compares a shutdown year with a producing one. The increase is the restart, sourced to the life-of-mine schedule [S14][F28], not a growth assumption.

flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.6 vs bull 1.2 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The asymmetry is the point of the bear case, not a thumb on the scale. The downside is an absorbing state: the disclosed money is raised at WRC and is applied first to WRC's own liabilities [S7], no lender for the subsidiary build is disclosed, and the licence expires on 7 September 2030 [S2], so a late or absent funding leaves the capex spent and the mine unbuilt — a total loss, which a mirrored 0.8 volume multiplier cannot express. The bull is capped at 1.2 because the same licence date caps the ounces that any amount of money can produce inside the window.

flags.message: expected return -44%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced facts produce the negative expected return, and none is a forecast we chose: the operating licence expires on 7 September 2030 [S2], so only 86 koz of the 738 koz IQPR schedule [S14][F28] can be mined and the Rp2,904bn escalated build cannot pay back inside the window; the disclosed money is raised at WRC and applied first to WRC's own liabilities, with no subsidiary lender named anywhere [S7][S11]; and the 2018 study escalated to 2026 dollars with the roasting capital charged [S14][S18] removes the margin the earlier work claimed. Today's price implies the market is paying for a licence extension and a completed funding that no filing evidences; the reverse DCF and the price-implied value are stated in section 4.

flags.message: the DCF stops after 5 years while reserves last ~81038 years at FY+1 volume: extend the horizon or justify the cut
flags.justification: The reserve/volume test divides 810.385 koz [F16] by the FY2026E run-off volume of 0.01 koz, which is meaningless in a restart year. The cut at five years is the licence, not the reserve: block one expires on 7 September 2030 [S2] and no filing evidences an extension application or a renewal, so scheduling ore after that date would capitalise unlicensed production — the red team's first fatal finding. Only 86 koz of the 738 koz IQPR schedule [S14][F28] can be mined inside the licensed window, and the report states plainly that the rest is carried at zero.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_life': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.3, 'pbv': 0.1}
flags.justification: Reweighted from the industry default because both multiple legs are unusable on a company with negative EBITDA, a book value eroded by Rp541bn of accumulated losses and no production [S2]; the method card for a commodity cyclical requires a through-cycle, life-of-asset approach.
